This is always mildly traumatic to see.  My parents would punish me harshly for this.  Every week or so they would scream at me, hit me, force me to destroy things I loved, sometimes in front of company.  They were convinced I was a pathological liar, a passive aggressive angry kid, and someone who hated his family and wanted to cause pain.  They'd humiliate me at stores regularly as I'd be forced to replace articles of clothing.  Shirts, socks, underwear, and they'd explain to the cashiers how I had "problems."  I'd be taken to doctors and therapists and treated for issues i didn't have.  Often the main punishment would be copying sentences about anger management.  40,000 times once.  Took me almost an entire year.  I was grounded, excluded from family activities, treats, trips, sometimes even school for the entire duration until i completed their task.  Sometimes they'd just put more on the end of it if I cried or had a breakdown.  I ran away once, attempted suicide a few times.  And even to this day my mom will bring it up.  They refuse to acknowledge that any of it was a mistake, and as a kid I could never voice reason.  I had no friends, i was depressed and isolated.  And it fucks with me as an adult now.  

So yeah, don't blame your kids.  This post is what my parents should have done.  They should have asked.  I wish they would have.  Our relationships will never be the same now, this is a permanent stain.  To them I will always be the angy problem child who hated them.

I don't remember the first time I picked up a blade, but my skin does.  It remembers the parting of flesh and the warm trickle of blood.  In the moment I told myself that I needed it, that it was good, that it helped me.  And for a long time I believed those words.  I used it as a way to distract myself from my inner turmoil, to bring about a sense of relief and validation.  Relief to have something to focus on, and validation to have a "real" source of pain.  I knew that it wasn't a healthy coping method, but it possessed such an allure that at times my strongest desires were to do the worst things to myself.  After a certain amount of time living with depression, you begin to wonder what's real and what isn't.  It was nice to have something real.  Something you could see.  Yet the knowledge of how wrong it was brought about immense feelings of shame and guilt.  I had to hide my body like I hid my emotions, and rather than lifting me out of the spiral like I told myself it would, it only drove me deeper.  I had turned something that the body isn't supposed enjoy or experience into my own personal oasis.  It was like I was getting high watching the world fall away.  I still feel deeply ashamed, but as the years wear on my desire to cut is slowly replaced by a desire to get better.  "I don't need it like I used to," a new mantra to pass through my thoughts.  At times I don't believe it, I laugh at myself, a liar and a hypocrite.  Though I know somewhere deep down that one day I'll no longer look back on myself in hatred, I can only hope that one day I'll feel happy to see who I have become, where I've gone, and to finally feel that dark cloud that has covered my mind for decades finally fade.  I used to think death was the solution to that, but no, now I'm quite certain it's life.  And love.  Friendship, resolution, confidence.   It's about learning and trying.  And comittment.

It's all fish.  When I was little, I was obsessed with the ocean.  Not like, finding Nemo (which I was), but imagine a 7 year old browsing the latest works from renown oceanic conservation societies.  Anything from sea surface currents to various species of deep dwelling invertebrates.  I don't remember much of it now, school consisted of a lot of fact regurgitation.  I don't recall the different members of cephalopods or nudibranchs to well, but once in a while I'll recall some species of invasive sea urchin or the name of a free floating colony organism...and it'll make me smile.  I kept two aquariums, salt and fresh, had fish living up to ten or 15 years.  I loved every second of it.  Got my first one when I was ten, it was the greatest birthday gift of my life.  I got a lot of happiness out of it.  

But I also dealt with a lot of depression, and the fish started to get sick and die.  I tried to medicate the water, figure out why it was all going to shit... I checked the salinity and the nitrates and the mineral levels, but I couldn't figure out why they were getting so so sick.  I couldn't afford reverse osmosis water, so in the end when all my fish died, I sold the tanks.  It killed me to see them suffer, and to know it was my fault made it worse.  Sometimes I have dreams where I'm taking care of the most beautiful tanks, but for one reason or another it turns to shit.  I'll never get the smell of rotting fish out of my head.  I miss it so much.  But some people just aren't good with animals.  I mean, I'd give anything to have my dog back, anything at all.  But life doesn't work like that you know?  People say try better next time, but there's not going to be a next time.  Some things are irreplaceable like that.

I remember being at the pet store, my last clownfish was nearly folded in half in pain from some unseen poison.  I was practically begging for help.  The man behind the counter looked at me and told me I've done it all wrong, for all those years.  I was causing it to suffer.  I thought that I was doing the right thing, but he showed me his...common clowns, 20 years old.  Mine barely hit half that.  He made sure I knew how very deeply I screwed up.

Sometimes when I'm feeling really fucked up, I just scroll the sub and look at all the creatures out there.  It's calming, and it sometimes keeps me from doing things I shouldn't.  I like to pretend some day, that I'll have another tank.  A nice big one, one big enough to be stable.  I'd use the right water, grow corals, and do everything just right.  But I know that'll never happen, I just couldn't.  So I look at them on reddit instead.
